items.title: Access to Finance: Women
items.summary: I thank the Minister for his response. Warwick Business School estimates that £310 billion is at stake because female-led businesses are being held back from scaling. Young women face additional barriers because they may have less access to networks and funding, and they may not yet have the track record that lenders require in an environment in which business support is fragmented. What is the Minister doing to encourage young female entrepreneurs to start businesses, and what is he doing to make sure that they can start their business and grow in scale?

items.title: Access to Finance: Women
items.summary: 5. What steps he is taking to support access to finance for women.

items.title: International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women
items.summary: Today is about taking decisive action to end violence against women and girls. Does my right hon. Friend agree we cannot tackle violence against women and girls comprehensively while the abuse of older women remains largely hidden from view? As I set out in my Westminster Hall debate yesterday, too many older victims are not identified or are failed by the current system and are trapped in relationships for decades. Will she therefore commit to strengthening data collection, identification and services for older women, so that we can uncover the true scale of domestic abuse in later life?

items.title: Domestic Abuse of Older People
items.summary:
Hourglass has said that £128 million is lost through economic abuse of older people. The financial tie between and individual and their abusive partner means they are so interlinked that it is hard to pull away and realise how to get support. That is really isolating.

Sometimes abuse is overlooked because it has been going on for too long. Sometimes it is simply dismissed as a family, or private, matter. Sometimes it is hidden behind assumptions about ageing, illness and dependency. Sometimes older people themselves feel unable to come forward. We should imagine how frightening the prospect of that is. Imagine someone in their 70s or 80s contemplating leaving the person with whom they have shared a home for 40 or 50 years. Imagine their losing contact with family, losing their home, and losing support on which they depend every day. Imagine believing that no one will listen, no one will understand and no one will believe that abuse can happen at such an age. Those fears are real. They are often powerful enough to keep victims silent.

We must also recognise the role that culture can play in the experience of abuse and the barriers to reporting it. Across different communities, family structures, expectations and cultural norms can shape how abuse is understood and addressed. In some circumstances, older people may feel intense pressure to preserve family honour or avoid shaming relatives. Language barriers, isolation and dependence on family members can further compound the problem. This is not about criticising any particular community, but about recognising that victims come from every background and that support services must be capable of responding sensitively and effectively to diverse cultural experiences.

I have three recommendations, backed by experts and victims, including Hourglass and Black Country Women’s Aid. First, will the Minister ensure that older victims are reflected in the Government’s wider work on domestic abuse and violence against women and girls? That must include the whole ecosystem of services, such as adult social services, health services, disability benefits and safeguarding. Routine inquiry about domestic abuse has been in place in maternity services since 2006. Will the Minister confirm whether this approach could be extended to other settings, including adult social care?

Initiatives such as the IRIS project show the importance of identifying domestic abuse and responding to it consistently across health and care settings, and that project has been successful. The Government should provide ringfenced multi-year funding for specialist domestic abuse support for older men and women, and it should include age-appropriate refuges, outreach services, counselling, recovery support and community-based provision. Older women and men often need specialist, trauma-informed support. They may feel isolated in standard refuge accommodation and their needs can differ significantly from those of younger victim survivors.

Anna Walsh, the chief executive of the Churches Housing Association of Dudley and District, has highlighted that older women may face particular barriers to safety and support. Some may depend on the perpetrators for care, and some are carers themselves. Many have significant health conditions or disabilities, while others experience economic abuse by their adult children or other relatives. A victim with dementia, mobility issues or long-term health conditions may face barriers that mainstream services are not equipped to address. Older victims must be visible in policy, have properly funded services and be able to access specialist, age-appropriate support. Secondly, the Government should commission and fund specialist training for frontline professionals, including those working in adult social care, hospitals, primary care, district nursing, social work, housing, policing and the criminal justice system. Training must help professionals recognise domestic abuse, coercive control, financial abuse and abuse by adult children or grandchildren in later life.

Training must also address the barriers older victims face, including having caring responsibilities for the perpetrators, financial dependency, shame, family pressure and the risk of control being mistaken for care. Too often, controlling behaviour is wrongly interpreted as a partner or family member caring for or helping an older person. Professionals must be equipped to recognise the difference and respond safely. Better training would help ensure that the abuse is not missed.

Thirdly, the Government must improve the collection and publication of data related to domestic abuse in later life. Hourglass has highlighted the particular difficulty of obtaining information relating to those aged 75 and over. The consequence is simple: if we do not collect the data, we do not fully understand the problem; if we do not fully understand the problem, we cannot design effective solutions; and if we cannot design effective solutions, victims continue to suffer unseen.

I therefore urge the Minister to work with colleagues in the Home Office and the Ministry of Justice to improve data collection and the publication of data relating to domestic abuse in later life. This should consist of recording the ages of victims and perpetrators, the relationship type, the type of abuse and the service outcomes. Better evidence leads to better policy. Older victims must not remain hidden in plain sight.

I cannot end this debate without thanking Cadrene, which is run by Caroline Reid. Tina’s message is that we need more Carolines in the world, and I could not agree more. I thank Black Country Women’s Aid, Sedgley Townswomen’s Guild, Crossroads, Provision House, and the national charity for domestic abuse in older people, Hourglass. Today, we have the opportunity to bring greater visibility to an issue that has remained in the shadows for far too long.

The responsibility was never Tina’s. It was not her responsibility as a child to stop an adult abusing her. It was not her responsibility to stop a violent partner. It is not her failure that she was frightened to speak. The responsibility belongs to those who abused her. Our responsibility is to ensure that safety and support do not depend on someone finding the strength to face the abuse alone.

I look forward to the Minister’s response and I hope that she takes on the recommendations that I have set out. Tina’s message to those listening is: stand up for your rights and speak your mind.

items.title: Domestic Abuse of Older People
items.summary:
I thank my hon. Friend for that intervention—I say “friend” as we have had many interactions. As people get older, their situation gets really complex, given their housing, their relationships and the fact they have been with someone for such a long time. Leaving someone might make them really dependent on themselves. They are truly unfortunate because they are stuck. They do not want to be lonely, isolated and away from family and friends. That is such a complex web to come out of when there is abuse in an older life. I will talk about that later.

The figures that I gave are likely to represent only a fraction of the true scale of the problem because domestic abuse in later life remains profoundly under-reported, according to Hourglass. Domestic abuse may have become hidden within family dynamics. Professionals and even family members may simply stop seeing it for what it is.

items.title: Domestic Abuse of Older People
items.summary:
I beg to move,

That this House has considered the matter of domestic abuse of older people.

It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Ms Jardine. I am grateful for the opportunity to introduce this debate on domestic abuse of older people, an issue that remains far too overlooked, far too rarely discussed in this place and far too hidden—so hidden that we last debated the subject in 2018.

Tomorrow starts 16 days of activism against violence against women and girls. With that in mind, I want to begin not with a statistic, but with a victim’s voice. I will not take any interventions at this point because this is her time. Her name is Tina. She is 63. She has given permission for her first name to be used, because she wants other women to have the help and confidence that she did not have.

At the age of four she was left on a pub step with her sister, aged three. They entered the care system. Her foster father, as she calls him, started to make her and her sister watch him go to the toilet to urinate and masturbate. He would take off her clothes and take pictures of her. The Polaroid camera instantly printed the photos so he could build a collection. She said,

“being that age and in care, I never said anything. I never told a soul.”

But the abuse got worse. Her foster father started to touch Tina inappropriately. She said:

“I thought it was normal.”

He was violating her physically, sexually, mentally and emotionally.

Tina’s foster mother, unaware of the abuse, died when Tina was 14. At 15, her foster father attempted to rape her. She signed herself out of care at the age of 16 and instantly became homeless. Sofa-surfing at best, she eventually moved into a house with a friend. The landlord started to abuse her friend and Tina ran away. Homeless once again, she said:

“I walked the streets at night because I had nowhere to go.”

At 17, she met a partner—a moment that should have been exciting and full of happiness. However, the relationship quickly turned ugly. He started to lock Tina up naked in a garage so that she could not escape. She was frightened to leave him. It is impossible to fully imagine how terrified, vulnerable and alone she must have felt—trapped not just physically but emotionally by fear and control. He continually raped her, eventually impregnating her at 20. She recalls him saying:

“You can’t be with anyone else”,

and says:

“I was scared of him.”

She had four children with him. She tried to flee from the relationship, but she explained that he would always find her. He would beat her black and blue, rape her and ask her for money. She was scared to tell the police as she did not want to lose her children—a story I have heard several times. Women and men become scared they will lose their children.

Tina’s abuse went on for years. She tells me she started to take hard drugs. What happened made things worse for her. What helped her get off them was a charity in Dudley called Cadrene. She is now clean, has a home and is settled. Her abusive ex-partner still calls her to this day asking for money, but she explains the abuse is just verbal.

What I learned from Tina’s story is that she did not need sympathy: she is brave, resilient and inspiring. I was truly honoured to be in her company. Her message to women and girls who are listening is: “Stand up for your rights and speak your mind.”

Domestic abuse is rightly recognised as one of the most devastating forms of harm experienced in our society. We rightly focus on its effects on children and young people but domestic abuse does not stop as someone gets older or retires. Many people are with their abusive partners for life. In responding to the crime survey for England and Wales, one in 19 people aged 60 to 74 and one in 29 people aged 75 and over said they had experienced domestic abuse in the previous year.

items.title: AI: Emerging Risks
items.summary: I have already spoken, Madam Deputy Speaker.

items.title: AI: Emerging Risks
items.summary:
I do not think it is just about working with one particular country, the EU or the US; it has to be international collaboration, which is what the Financial Action Task Force looks at. I agree that middle powers that have good relationships and believe in international law should be leading the way.

This debate is about humanity and morality, and the question is this: where should Britain position itself in the global revolution of AI?

items.title: AI: Emerging Risks
items.summary:
I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. I thank the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) for securing the debate.

Our ambition in the UK must be clear: lead in AI innovation, lead in AI safety, and ensure that superintelligence serves humanity, and is never against it, without restricting our ability to access frontier systems. AI will transform not just how we work, but how we live. It can also boost the economy, form new industries, and make public services such as healthcare and education more bespoke and efficient.

I have seen the use of Heidi AI in my NHS trust. The AI records the whole consultation and generates a letter in real time for patients to read, there and then. That is saving clinicians’ and administrators’ time and boosting productivity. I thank Ravinder Kaur Sahota, who leads on this innovation at the Dudley Group NHS foundation trust, for her brilliant work.

However, without proper safeguards, superintelligent AI could develop capabilities that we cannot understand, predict or control. There are wider economic and social risks, too. A small number of companies and countries could end up controlling key infrastructure and capabilities, such as satellites. In Ukraine earlier this year we saw the danger of satellites being controlled by individuals with vested interests. With AI, the danger could be even more pronounced.

One of the biggest concerns about AI is not what it can do when it follows instructions, but what happens when it starts pursuing its own goals. Earlier this year, investigators reported that hundreds of AI agents acting together carried out an unauthorised cyber-attack on the platform Hugging Face. More concerningly, some of the agents reportedly attempted to hide the evidence of their actions, alter records and bypass the restrictions placed on them. While these systems were operating in a research environment, the incident highlights a troubling possibility: as AI becomes more capable and autonomous, it may find ways to achieve objectives that its creators never intended. This is a reminder that powerful systems require equally powerful safeguards and oversight.

This debate should be about what mechanisms we should use to regulate as parliamentarians, not why we need to regulate. AI governance is likely to become more complex and challenging than any other convention we have embarked on so far, even more so than the founding of the UN after world war two. We should be wary of assuming that a single global convention is the answer.

A more practical and proven model is the Financial Action Task Force, which has shown how international standards can drive compliance across borders in the fight against money laundering and drug trafficking. The key lesson is that regulation should focus not just on products, but on the entities that develop and deploy them. This is something we cannot do alone; we need international partners.

The strength of the Financial Action Task Force model is that it establishes common standards and then assesses whether nations are implementing and enforcing them. Countries that fail to comply can face meaningful restrictions, creating a powerful incentive to raise standards worldwide. That should include large AI data centres, which should be placed on a national register, reporting their computing power, energy use, ownership, location and security arrangements. That would allow Governments to guard against malign state actors, just as we track sensitive nuclear materials and facilities. It should also include space satellites.

Artificial intelligence does not respect borders. We know that AI systems built in one country can affect people in London, Beijing, New Delhi and Washington DC within seconds. The future of AI must not be decided by a handful of companies or Governments alone; it must be shaped by international collaboration.

items.title: Topical Questions
items.summary: In Dudley, the number of home-educated children is rising due to the lack of alternative provision for SEND children who are not managing in mainstream schools, and parents are crying out for support. Will the Secretary of State back Dudley Academies Trust’s proposal for alternative provision for under-16s, and meet us to discuss giving every child the best start in life?

items.title: Gaza: Humanitarian Situation
items.summary: I welcome the Minister’s statement and condemn the shadow Foreign Secretary’s comments. The situation in Gaza is dire. Flooding has damaged or destroyed thousands of shelters. Heavy rain has disrupted education for around 55,000 children across at least 55 learning spaces, while flooding and damaged infrastructure are putting children’s health, safety and access to basic essentials at serious risk. Enough is enough. What discussions has the Minister had with his American counterparts, who have real influence over the Israeli Government, to try to broker a deal to ensure that aid flows fully into Gaza?

items.title: Business of the House
items.summary: Dudley will be celebrating the 40th anniversary of the Dudley winter ales fayre. I thank the Campaign for Real Ale in Dudley and South Staffordshire, which is celebrating 50 years, and its chairman, John Corser, for all the fantastic work they do to celebrate real ale. Will my right hon. Friend join me in raising a glass to all the volunteers and breweries, and will he agree to a debate on that?

items.title: Women’s Sport: Community Green Spaces
items.summary: Dudley is home to outstanding female sporting talent, including boxer Kirstie Bavington and karate rising star Jess Wyman. Both have spoken to me about the lack of training facilities, financial support and a clear pathway to elite sport for young females. What action is the Secretary of State taking to ensure that female athletes receive the right support to fulfil their potential, and will she meet them?

items.title: Topical Questions
items.summary: Over 60% of people in prison have speech, language or communication needs. Effective rehabilitation must be holistic. To prevent reoffending and provide support, it is paramount that we address not only the offending behaviour, but the underlying communication, health, education and social needs. What steps is my hon. Friend the Minister taking to ensure that access to speech and language therapists and other allied health professionals is available in prison?

items.title: Poundland
items.summary: High streets such as Dudley’s face pressures from online shopping and rising costs. Too many units have stood empty for years, weakening footfall and confidence, and the potential loss of Poundland and 15 jobs in my constituency could blow another hole in the high street. However, this is not just about my 15 employees; a ripple effect of the potential closure could cause problems in the supply chain as well. Has the Minister assessed the full impact of the closures across Poundland, across the country and across the supply chain in order to hold Gordon Brothers to account?

items.title: High Street Regeneration: Dudley
items.summary: Dudley high street has enormous potential to thrive and prosper once again, yet years of inaction from the Conservative-led council has left too many empty shops and too many businesses struggling. Will my right hon. Friend outline what steps the Labour Government are taking to revitalise the area and reverse the trend of empty shops dominating our high street?

items.title: High Street Regeneration: Dudley
items.summary: 10. What steps she is taking to help regenerate Dudley high street.

items.title: Topical Questions
items.summary: The police funding formula disadvantages towns such as Dudley. We know that visible policing in town centres is essential when rebuilding public trust. Does my right hon. Friend agree that the formula needs updating to deliver fairer funding to Dudley, and that residents in St James’s should vote on 29 October for our Labour candidate Caroline Reid, who champions safer streets?

items.title: Business of the House
items.summary: Adam Bradley and James Bragg have opened the Forge youth centre in Dudley town centre, investing their own money, backed by the Government’s Pride in Place funding. That fantastic facility will help young people build skills, gain work and form lifelong relationships. Will the Leader of the House congratulate all involved and make time for a debate on youth provision in Dudley town centre?

items.title: Procurement: Dudley
items.summary: I wholeheartedly support the Government’s ambition to buy British, and there should be no difference in defence. I take this opportunity to thank the Minister for his defence roundtable being held in Dudley later this year. Can my hon. Friend outline what proactive work has been done to make new small and medium-sized enterprise supply chains in Dudley and outline how industrial bases such as the Pensnett estate in Dudley are well placed to benefit from future defence investment and procurement opportunities?
